title: Exact iteration count of the entry's Hungarian implementation: row-monotone worst case and rectangular counts
statement: For the successive-shortest-augmenting-path Hungarian code of pairs/assignment-brute-vs-hungarian (rows inserted one at a time; an iteration is one pass of its inner loop, which evaluates cur = C[i0][j] - u[i0] - v[j] for every unused column j and selects the smallest index among the unused columns with minimal minv) and its rectangular form (rows 1..m, columns 1..n, m <= n): Lemma 1: on every input, the search for row i runs at most i iterations and iteration t evaluates cur exactly n - t + 1 times, so at most m(m+1)/2 iterations and m(m+1)(3n - m + 1)/6 = (n+1)m(m+1)/2 - m(m+1)(m+2)/6 evaluations. Theorem 2: on every integer (or exact rational) matrix with non-decreasing rows, the search for row i runs exactly i iterations, selecting columns 1..i-1 and then column i. Corollary 3: these matrices attain the maxima of Lemma 1 exactly (n(n+1)/2 iterations and n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 evaluations for n x n), including the entry's timing family C[i][j] = 1000 j + r, r in 0..999. Proposition 4: for m <= n with non-decreasing rows, an optimal assignment uses only the first m columns, so the square code on the m x m submatrix (m(m+1)(2m+1)/6 evaluations) replaces the full run (m(m+1)(3n - m + 1)/6). Proposition 5: adding M j to column j (columns 1..n, M > max C - min C) makes rows strictly increasing and shifts every permutation's cost by M n(n+1)/2, so any algorithm for square row-monotone inputs solves every square input with O(n^2) additional unit-cost operations. Proposition 6: on every integer (or exact rational) square matrix the square code returns the minimum assignment cost.

bases: Folklore: O(n) iterations per inserted row, hence O(n^3) (O(n^2 m) for rectangular inputs), for this implementation of the Hungarian method; read in the cp-algorithms article 'Hungarian algorithm for solving the assignment problem', which presents the C++ code that the entry transcribes
Edmonds-Karp 1972 (J. ACM 19(2), doi:10.1145/321694.321699), abstract: O(n^3) for the n x n assignment problem; no per-row or exact iteration counts

sources.note: Base: the only source read that states the per-row bound for this implementation. Presents the C++ code that the entry transcribes (developed by Andrey Lopatin, per the article), 'Each row is processed in time O(n^2), since only O(n) potential recalculations could occur', O(n^3), and O(n^2 m) for rectangular inputs. The passages on the O(n^3) algorithm and the implementation were read.
